analysis.one_liner: Accelerates earlier tax cuts, exempts most stock dividends from income tax, and expands small-business equipment deductions.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee reported the bill favorably in May 2003 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it; a smaller, differently structured tax cut became law that month instead.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would move up tax cuts originally scheduled for later years: lower income-tax rates, a bigger 10% bracket, marriage-penalty relief, a $1,000 child tax credit, and higher alternative-minimum-tax exemptions. It would also exempt a large share of corporate stock dividends from income tax, let small businesses immediately deduct up to $75,000 of equipment and software purchases, and send federal money to states for health care, schools, and infrastructure. To offset some of the cost, it adds penalties and reporting rules aimed at abusive tax shelters and corporate tax avoidance.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children get the child credit raised to $1,000 right away, including an advance refund check in 2003; married couples get faster marriage-penalty relief; taxpayers exposed to the alternative minimum tax get a bigger exemption for 2003-2005; and small businesses can deduct equipment and off-the-shelf software immediately. The largest dollar benefits, however, flow to shareholders through the dividend exclusion, since stock ownership is concentrated among higher-income households, and to high earners through the faster reduction of the top income-tax rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shareholders, high earners, families with children

how_it_helps.text: Accelerates the child tax credit to $1,000 per child starting in 2003 and requires advance refund checks to eligible families before the end of 2003.
Speeds up all the 2001 income-tax rate cuts to 2003, including lowering the top rate from 38.6% to 35%, and expands the 10% bracket and marriage-penalty relief.
Raises the alternative minimum tax exemption amounts for 2003 through 2005, shielding many middle- and upper-middle-income households from a tax originally aimed at the wealthy.
Raises the small-business expensing allowance to $75,000 (with a phaseout starting at $325,000) and lets businesses immediately expense off-the-shelf computer software.
Authorizes federal payments to states for job training, health care, transportation, law enforcement, and essential services, and increases Medicaid payments through 2004.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue falls, so the cuts are paid for by borrowing and by future taxpayers; the dividend exclusion in particular directs most of its value to households that own stock, while the offset provisions raise new penalties but not enough to cover the cost of the tax cuts.

drawbacks.text: The largest provisions — the accelerated top-rate cuts and the dividend exclusion — deliver most of their dollar value to higher-income households, since high earners pay the top rates and stock ownership is concentrated among wealthier families.

Exempting dividends from income tax requires elaborate new rules for corporations, funds, insurers, and foreign shareholders (the bill text runs through dozens of special cases), adding major complexity to the tax code to benefit one form of investment income.
The bill would prohibit states from using children's health insurance funds to cover childless adults (other than pregnant women), narrowing who the safety-net program can reach.
Almost every provision sunsets after 2012, meaning the tax code would revert automatically — a design choice that made the long-term cost look smaller than it really was.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The family and small-business provisions deliver real, immediate help, including refund checks to families in 2003 and AMT relief. But the bill's center of gravity is the dividend exclusion and accelerated top-rate cuts, whose benefits are heavily concentrated among high-income households, and the revenue losses add to federal borrowing. The bill does make a genuine effort at offsets — new penalties on tax shelters and Enron-style transactions — but those do not approach the size of the tax cuts.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee reported the bill to the floor in May 2003, but Senate leaders instead moved a companion tax cut through a House bill, so S.2 sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Don Nickles introduced the bill on February 27, 2003, 'by request' of the administration, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

On May 8, 2003, the Finance Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on May 9 Senator Grassley reported it and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders.

The reported version would have accelerated the 2001 tax cuts to 2003, raised the alternative minimum tax exemption for 2003-2005, increased small-business expensing to $75,000, excluded a portion of dividends from income tax, added tax-shelter penalties and Enron-related provisions, and provided federal aid and Medicaid increases to states.
No further action is recorded: the bill never received a Senate floor vote, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The tax cut enacted in May 2003 — the Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act — was roughly half the size of what the president originally sought and taxed dividends at a reduced 15% rate rather than exempting them entirely.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy shareholders came out ahead either way — they still received a dividend tax cut through the smaller law enacted in May 2003, though not the full exclusion this bill offered. Tax shelter promoters also avoided the bill's new penalties, and the federal treasury avoided a larger revenue loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy shareholders, shelter promoters, the treasury

for.name: Sen. Don Nickles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill 'by request' on February 27, 2003, and recruited six Republicans and one Democrat to cosponsor it.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance (chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley)
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill and reported it favorably on May 9, 2003, with a substitute amendment rewriting much of its content, placing it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: The bill was introduced by request, meaning it was submitted on the administration's behalf; the president was publicly pushing for an accelerated tax cut and a dividend tax cut at the time.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and party leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled S.2 for a Senate floor vote after it was reported to the calendar; the Senate instead took up the companion tax cut through a House bill, which passed at about half the original requested size after moderates insisted on the smaller figure.

against.name: Senate moderates and Democrats
against.role: Bipartisan group of senators who demanded a smaller package
against.what_they_did: Insisted during the 2003 debate that the tax cut be capped at roughly $350 billion and opposed the full dividend exclusion, forcing the final law to use a reduced 15% dividend rate instead.

sides.party_line_note: Six of the bill's seven cosponsors were Republicans, and the underlying fight over the size and design of the 2003 tax cut split largely along party lines, with a handful of moderate Republicans forcing the smaller final package.

industries.note: The bill would exclude most corporate dividends from income tax and accelerate the cut in top income-tax rates; because stock ownership and top-bracket income are concentrated among wealthier households, most of this value flows to them, financed by federal borrowing. Ordinary families do get the child credit and AMT relief, but the largest dollar benefits are wealth-skewed.
The expensing allowance would rise to $75,000 and off-the-shelf software would become immediately deductible, letting small businesses write off equipment purchases in the year they are made.

industries.industry: Tax shelter promoters and their advisors
industries.note: The bill imposes new penalties and reporting requirements on reportable and noneconomic-substance transactions, requires material advisors to register deals, and lets the IRS pursue promoters of abusive shelters — provisions that make tax-avoidance schemes riskier.

Federal appropriations would fund job training, health care, transportation, and public safety in the states, with increased Medicaid payments through 2004, easing state budget shortfalls during the post-recession squeeze.

The dividend exclusion and repeal of the accumulated earnings and personal holding company taxes would benefit corporations and their owners, and the bill would let sports franchises amortize intangibles and ease some bankruptcy-related loss limits; new executive compensation rules cut the other way for insiders.

The bill writes detailed special rules for how life, property, and mutual insurers handle the dividend exclusion, and sets mutual life insurers' differential earnings rate to zero through 2008 — a package of adjustments with gains and losses for the industry.
